ECON.01.note: Open Yale Courses develops game theory through players, strategies, payoffs, information, timing, dominance, equilibrium, repeated interaction and applications rather than presenting it as a collection of puzzles.

exercise.prompt: Model one strategic situation by listing players, available actions, payoffs, information, order of moves and whether commitments are credible.

ECON.02.note: Yale's opening lecture derives the Prisoner's Dilemma from its payoff structure and uses it to distinguish individually dominant choices from collectively better outcomes.

deeper.title: Lecture 21 — Repeated Games: Cooperation versus the End Game

exercise.prompt: Write a Prisoner's Dilemma payoff matrix, identify dominant strategies and equilibrium, then change repetition, patience and punishment to make cooperation sustainable.

ECON.03.note: Yale's lecture introduces best responses and Nash equilibrium while emphasizing that equilibrium means no profitable unilateral deviation, not fairness, efficiency or happiness.

article.title: Lecture 5 — Nash Equilibrium: Bad Fashion and Bank Runs

exercise.prompt: Find every pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in three small payoff matrices and identify which equilibria are Pareto-efficient, risky or coordination-dependent.

ECON.04.note: The Nobel overview explains Schelling's work on tacit coordination, focal points, credible commitments, conflict and segregation without reducing it to a party-game trick.

article.title: Conflict and Cooperation through the Lens of Game Theory

exercise.prompt: Give several people the same no-communication meeting problem, compare their chosen focal points, and explain which shared conventions made one answer salient.

ECON.05.note: The Nobel overview contrasts simple privatization-or-state-control prescriptions with Ostrom's evidence that communities can build durable institutions for shared resources under identifiable conditions.

article.title: Economic Governance: The Organization of Cooperation

exercise.prompt: Design governance rules for one shared resource covering boundaries, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, local participation and adaptation over time.

ECON.06.note: Yale's lecture treats moral hazard as hidden action after a contract and separates it from adverse selection, incentives, monitoring and risk sharing.

exercise.prompt: Design an insurance or employment contract that balances risk protection with incentives, then identify behaviours the principal cannot directly observe.

ECON.07.note: The IMF explanation derives gains from trade through opportunity cost and specialization, including the counterintuitive case where one country is absolutely more productive in every activity.

exercise.prompt: Give two producers different productivities in two goods, calculate opportunity costs, choose specialization and show a trade price that benefits both.

ECON.08.note: The 2020 Nobel overview connects auction formats, private and common values, the winner's curse, bidding strategies and the design of real spectrum auctions.

article.title: The Quest for the Perfect Auction

exercise.prompt: Run first-price and second-price sealed-bid auctions with private values, compare truthful and shaded bidding, then add uncertain common value to create a winner's-curse risk.

ECON.09.note: The Bank of England explains that commercial-bank lending creates matching deposits, while repayment destroys bank money and central-bank reserves play a different settlement role.

article.title: Money Creation in the Modern Economy

exercise.prompt: Write simplified bank and borrower balance sheets before a loan, immediately after lending, after spending and after principal repayment, tracking deposits, loans and reserves.

ECON.10.note: The Stanford study examines technology adoption when a product becomes more valuable as compatible users grow, separating installed-base effects from product quality and marketing.

article.title: Adoption of Technologies with Network Effects: An Empirical Examination of the Adoption of Automated Teller Machines
article.source: Garth Saloner and Andrea Shepard — Stanford Graduate School of Business

exercise.prompt: Model adoption of a platform whose value rises with users, then test how interoperability, multi-homing, switching cost, subsidies and congestion alter winner-take-most dynamics.

ECON.11.note: The Nobel overview presents Spence's signalling model, where education or another observable action can convey hidden productivity only when its costs differ across types.

exercise.prompt: Construct a separating signal by assigning different signal costs to high- and low-quality types, then show when pooling or imitation destroys credibility.

ECON.12.note: The Nobel explanation presents mechanism design as reverse game theory: define desired outcomes, information constraints and incentives, then design rules that make truthful or socially useful behaviour rational.

exercise.prompt: Design rules for allocating one scarce resource when participants privately know their values, then test incentive compatibility, efficiency, budget balance and participation.
